The Delta State Government says it is prosecuting more than 15 human trafficking cases, warning that traditional rulers must help expose traffickers and prevent the exploitation of children in their communities. The Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Ekemejero Ohwovoriole, SAN, disclosed this during an advocacy meeting with members of the Delta State Traditional Rulers Council on Thursday. Ohwovoriole, who is also Chairman of the Delta State Taskforce on Human Trafficking and Irregular Migration, said the government was committed to ending human trafficking through the enforcement of the Delta State Human Trafficking (Prohibition) Law, 2024. He urged traditional rulers to use their influence to identify suspicious activities, educate residents and encourage victims to report cases of trafficking. The meeting, organised under the theme, “The Royal Voice Against Human Trafficking: Protect Our Children, Preserve Our Culture,” focused on strengthening community efforts to prevent trafficking, protect victims and prosecute offenders. Your influence and standing make you vital partners in this fight. That is why we are here to seek your support and partnership,” he said. He warned that traffickers often deceive young people with promises of football trials, scholarships, employment, and better opportunities in major cities within and outside Nigeria. According to him, some victims are later subjected to exploitation after being lured with such promises. Nwoko’s supporter injured during APC primary dies NDC vows to resist attempts to intimidate Obi Delta violence: Reps urge Tinubu to intervene Ohwovoriole also identified the misuse of traditional practices, including forced oaths and threats of spiritual consequences, as tactics used by traffickers to silence victims and their families. He stressed that no cultural or traditional practice should be used to intimidate victims, conceal crimes or prevent them from seeking justice. The commissioner urged traditional rulers to discourage the use of shrines and traditional oaths to threaten victims, adding that rescued persons should be welcomed back into their communities without discrimination. He said victims needed love, understanding and support to rebuild their lives rather than being blamed or stigmatised for their experiences. He also called on the monarchs to encourage residents to report suspected trafficking cases to the appropriate authorities, warning that everyone involved in the illegal trade would face the law. Responding, the Chairman of the Delta State Traditional Rulers Council and Orodje of Okpe Kingdom, His Royal Majesty, Major General Felix Mujakperuo (retd.), Orhue I, pledged the council’s support for the government’s efforts. He warned that traffickers and their accomplices would be exposed and made to face the law. The monarch also urged community leaders and residents to remain vigilant, identify suspicious activities and report individuals suspected of engaging in human trafficking. Efecha Gold
